cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (assamica) cultivars; gongfu, Golden Bud or old-tree black material depending on the maker
processing: Finished Dian Hong (sometimes sun-dried shai hong) is lightly steamed, hand-rolled into single-serving balls of roughly 6–8 g, wrapped in tissue and dried again at low temperature.
harvest_season: Made from spring leaf for the better lots; autumn material is common in cheaper balls.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly irregular hand-rolled spheres of dark leaf and golden tips, each wrapped in white paper.
appearance_liquor: Bright orange-red, deepening to ruby as the ball opens fully.
appearance_wet: The ball loosens into whole twisted leaves and buds by the third steep.
taste_profile: Malt, honey and sweet potato like the loose tea it is made from, slightly rounder and quieter in aroma from the pressing, with a long sweet finish.

brewing.notes: One ball per session. Rinse 10–20 seconds to loosen it, then keep steeps short; the first two are pale, the middle ones are the best. One ball also does a 400 ml thermos for the day.

vintage_note: Sold by the year of the material, usually the current or previous spring; balls of ordinary Dian Hong are best within a year or two, while shai hong or old-tree balls are kept and sold with their vintage like small cakes.
description:
Dragon balls are the single-serving format of Yunnan black: a day's tea, around six to eight grams, hand-rolled into a sphere and wrapped in paper. The format came from sheng pu-erh, where it took off in the 2010s, and black-tea makers in Lincang and Xishuangbanna quickly adopted it because Dian Hong leaf is big, pliable and holds a shape well.

The balls are rolled from finished tea, not from fresh leaf: the dried Dian Hong is briefly steamed to soften it, pressed into a sphere by hand, wrapped and dried again gently. What goes in decides what you get – ordinary gongfu leaf, all-bud Golden Buds, old-tree material or sun-dried shai hong are all sold this way – and the light pressing rounds the aroma a little without changing the taste much.

Brewing is simple but needs patience. One ball in a 120–150 ml gaiwan, a rinse of ten to twenty seconds to crack it open, then short steeps: the first two are pale because the ball is still closed, the third to sixth are the best, and a good ball runs to eight or more. Boiling-ish water is fine. People who judge a ball on steep one are judging the wrapping, not the tea.

It is a convenience product, and the price per gram is a little above the same loose tea. Buy by what is inside: a shop should say whether the ball is plantation gongfu, Golden Bud, old-tree or shai hong, and from which year. Avoid balls that shed dust or come apart in the hand, which means over-dry, broken leaf was used.

They are the easiest way to take a proper Yunnan black to the office or on a trip; drop one in a thermos and top it up through the day.
sources_note: Ball weight and the steaming-and-rolling method are generalised from how Yunnan vendors describe their dragon balls; some makers roll fresh oxidised leaf before the final drying instead.
